notes:
Notes on Acts 20, verse by verse. I ran out of research calls before I could read the second half of the Enduring Word page and the later parts of some other commentaries, so verses 25 and 33–38 have little or no material. What's missing is listed at the end.

---

**v. 1**
- **Why Paul left.** Guzik says the riot in Ephesus convinced Paul to move west to Macedonia, and that he couldn't go without showing love to the believers there. (enduringword.com) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- **A different view.** Utley says Paul didn't leave because of the riot. He left because his evangelistic work there was done. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 2**
- **Where "that area" was.** Guzik suggests this could be when Paul visited Illyricum (Rom 15:19), which Acts never mentions directly. He adds that Acts is not a complete record of the first century. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- **Greece.** Utley says "Greece" means the province of Achaia, mainly Corinth, and that Paul wrote Romans during this stay. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 3**
- **The plot.** Utley thinks Paul may have planned to sail on a pilgrim ship carrying Jews to the feasts, and judged that unwise once the plot came out. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- Guzik quotes Williams: the attack may have been planned for on board, especially on a ship crowded with pilgrims. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**v. 4**
- **Who these men were.** Both Guzik and Utley see them as delegates from the churches, travelling with the collection for the poor in Jerusalem. Guzik adds that they could vouch for Paul's honest handling of the money. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/ ; https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- **Rich and poor together.** Guzik notes that "Aristarchus" suggests an aristocratic family, while "Secundus" ("Second") was a common slave name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**v. 5**
- **"Us."** The "we" passages start again here, meaning Luke rejoins Paul as an eyewitness. Utley lists all the "we" sections in Acts. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**v. 6**
- **The feast.** Utley says Luke may mention the Feast of Unleavened Bread simply because Paul was timing his journey to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost (v. 16). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 7: "First day of the week… to break bread"** *(debated)*
- **Traditional reading.** The meeting seems to have been in the evening, because Sunday was an ordinary working day for them. Guzik calls this the first certain example of Christians regularly meeting on the first day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- Utley calls "breaking bread" a New Testament idiom for the Lord's Supper. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- Gill says it was not an ordinary meal but the Eucharist. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/acts/20-7.html
- **Weekly communion.** Ray Van Neste (TGC) says Luke directly states the purpose of the meeting was the Lord's Supper, and argues from this for weekly communion. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/three-arguments-for-weekly-communion/
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) goes further: this verse states the purpose of Sunday gatherings all through history, namely the Lord's Supper. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/20-7.html
- Ellicott concludes that breaking the bread is an essential part of the sacrament, which may not be left out. https://biblehub.com/acts/20-7.htm
- **Saturday evening?** A translators' handbook (Newman and Nida, cited by Utley) reads this as Jewish time-keeping, so Saturday evening; the TEV/GNT translation follows that. Utley notes most translations stay literal. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 8**
- **The lamps.** Utley pictures a hot, smoky room and thinks Luke may be explaining why Eutychus fell asleep. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- Vincent mentions Hobart's view that listing the causes (heat, lamps, length, late hour) sounds like a doctor's account. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/20-9.htm

**v. 9: Was Eutychus to blame? Did he really die?**
- **Blame.** Calvin says Luke clears Eutychus, since he was overcome by deep sleep after midnight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/acts-20.html
- Matthew Henry is sterner: sleeping during preaching shows a low regard for God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/20-9.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says there is no need to blame either Eutychus or Paul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-20.html
- Guzik cites Hughes: the Greek verb tenses suggest Eutychus fought to stay awake. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- **Death.** The Expositor's Greek Testament says the words state plainly that he was dead, not "as if" dead. Vincent: "Actually dead." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/20-9.htm
- One Pulpit homily admits the text doesn't strictly rule out his being badly stunned. Even so, it says the simplest reading is a real death and restoration. https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/20-9.htm

**v. 10**
- **Elijah and Elisha.** Utley says Paul acted like Elijah and Elisha raising the dead (1 Kgs 17:21; 2 Kgs 4:34). https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- **"He is still alive."** Guzik quotes Marshall: this describes the boy after Paul ministered to him, and Luke would not record someone who only seemed dead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- **A charismatic note.** Guzik sees Paul receiving the gift of faith that God would raise the boy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- **Echo of Jesus.** The Pulpit Commentary compares Jesus' words, "The child is not dead, but sleepeth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-20.html

**v. 11**
- **Two meals?** Utley reads v. 11 as a shared fellowship meal alongside the Lord's Supper. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- **Teaching resumed.** Guzik says Paul got their attention back and preached until daybreak. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**v. 12**
- **"Boy."** Utley says the word for "boy" here differs from the "young man" of v. 9. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- Precept Austin suggests he may still have been a little dazed. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-20-commentary

**v. 13**
- **Paul on foot.** Guzik quotes Bruce: Paul likely stayed to the last moment to be sure Eutychus had fully recovered, then took a shortcut by land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- Utley suggests Paul may have wanted to know who was on the ship before boarding, given the earlier plot. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**vv. 14–15**
- **Places.** Utley notes Mitylene was the chief city of Lesbos, and remarks on Luke's technical sailing vocabulary. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 16**
- **Not a snub.** Guzik says Paul knew he could never make a *short* visit to Ephesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- Calvin notes that by calling the elders to Miletus, Paul showed he hadn't neglected Asia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/acts-20.html

**v. 17: Elders** *(church-government debate)*
- **Elders and bishops are the same.** Utley says Acts 20:17 and 20:28 show that "elders," "bishops/overseers" and "pastors" name one office. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- TGC (Reformed/evangelical) agrees that the two terms are used for the same group. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/the-role-of-the-elder-bishop-pastor/
- **Anglican view.** Ellicott agrees the terms were interchangeable then. But he adds that Paul stood toward these men as later bishops stood toward their elders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/20-17.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says it is generally agreed these were not diocesan bishops "in the modern Anglican sense." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-20.html
- **Catholic view.** Catholic Answers agrees the same men are called *presbyteroi* and *episkopoi*. It argues "presbyter" is the technical name of their ordained office, while "overseer" only describes their kind of ministry. https://www.catholic.com/qa/where-in-the-new-testament-are-priests-mentioned
- The Catholic Encyclopedia treats them as "presbyter-bishops" appointed by the Spirit. It doubts Irenaeus's claim that Paul called both bishops and presbyters to Miletus. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/07326a.htm

**vv. 18–19**
- **Paul as pastor.** Guzik says this is the one place Acts shows Paul as a pastor rather than an evangelist. Paul points to himself as an example in following Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/
- **Critics in the background.** Utley thinks the strong wording suggests Paul had critics. He calls humility a distinctly Christian virtue. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 20**
- **"Did not shrink."** Utley calls this a sailing term. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344
- **"House to house."** Guzik reads this as a sign that the Ephesian church met in house churches, each elder perhaps leading one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**v. 21**
- **No limits.** Guzik says Paul limited neither his message nor his audience. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**vv. 22–23: Spirit and prophecy**
- Guzik says Paul had apparently already received many prophetic warnings. He was not moved by uncertainty or danger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**v. 24**
- **Images.** Guzik draws out two pictures: Paul as an accountant weighing costs, and Paul as a runner finishing his own race. He uses Spurgeon's phrase, a gospel "worth dying for." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

**vv. 26–27: "Innocent of the blood… the whole will of God"**
- **What "blood" means.** John Piper (Baptist) says "blood" here means being lost eternally, not physical death. If any of them is lost, it won't be Paul's fault. He adds that this doesn't mean someone must know the whole counsel to be saved. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-guilt-of-giving-part-of-gods-counsel
- **Ezekiel's watchman.** GotQuestions links this to the watchman of Ezekiel 33. https://www.gotquestions.org/whole-counsel-of-God.html
- **What "the whole counsel" covers.** Gill says it means God's revealed will in the gospel, not his hidden decrees. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/acts/20-27.html
- Barnes says Paul didn't hide any truth out of fear or a wish to be popular. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/acts/20-27.html
- Clarke stresses what God has revealed about salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/acts-20.html

**v. 28: Overseers, and "His own blood"** *(debated)*
- **Watch yourselves first.** Precept Austin, citing Barnes and Baxter's *Reformed Pastor*, says leaders must guard their own hearts before guarding the flock. MacArthur sums up the speech as five priorities for elders. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts_2028-38_commentary
- **The textual question.** Some manuscripts read "church of the Lord" instead of "church of God." Clarke grants the evidence may favour "of the Lord," but insists that unless this Lord were God, his blood couldn't redeem anyone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/20-28.html
- Gill and Matthew Henry take the verse as proof that Christ is God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/20-28.html
- **"Blood of his own Son."** Some explain "his own blood" this way (see the Bible Hub page). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/20-28.htm Constable (via Precept Austin) prefers this rendering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts_2028-38_commentary The NET Bible's translation reads it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/acts/20-28.html
- **Reformed reading.** Calvin uses the verse to show Christ is one person, against Nestorius. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/acts-20.html
- A Bible Hub article draws "particular redemption" from it: Christ's blood was effective for a definite people. https://biblehub.com/q/Acts_20_28_Church_s_divine_purchase.htm
- **Wesleyan-type reading.** Another commentary on the Bible Hub page says only the Holy Spirit can make an overseer. It describes the church as only the believing, obedient, holy children of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/20-28.htm

**vv. 29–30**
- **The wolves.** Precept Austin calls them Satan's "servants of righteousness." https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts_2028-38_commentary
- On v. 30 it notes Paul uses a Greek perfect tense, which it takes to mean their words are permanently twisted. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-20-commentary

**v. 31**
- **For leaders today.** Precept Austin asks whether leaders today are warning their people as Paul did. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-20-commentary

**v. 32**
- **The word's power.** Precept Austin stresses that the word of grace is itself able to build believers up. It describes the "inheritance" as bought by Christ's blood and kept for believers. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-20-commentary

**v. 33**
- **Defending himself.** Utley reads this verse as Paul defending himself against personal attacks. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21344

**v. 35**
- **"Hard work."** The Greek word means effort to the point of sweat and exhaustion (Precept Austin). https://temp.preceptaustin.org/acts-20-commentary
- **Jesus' saying.** The Pulpit Commentary notes this saying isn't in our Gospels and was probably passed down by word of mouth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/acts-20.html

**On the whole speech (modern scholarship)**
- Some critical scholars (Baur, Zeller, Weizsäcker) argued Luke composed the speech, because it resembles the Pastoral Epistles. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary disputes this. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/acts-20.html
- Bruce (via Guzik) notes it is the only speech of Paul to Christians that Luke records, and it is full of parallels to Paul's letters. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-20/

---

**What I couldn't find**
- Anything on verse 25 or verses 36–38.
- Lutheran or Orthodox readings.
- NET Bible study notes (I only have the NET's wording of v. 28).
- Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on v. 35 or v. 24.
- Commentary on vv. 21–38 from the Enduring Word and bible.org pages, because both pages were cut off when I fetched them. The second half of the Enduring Word page is worth reading directly.
